analogy.p: Imagine a sieve with holes of a certain size. Rocks of mixed sizes are poured in; only those small enough pass through. Pour the passed-through rocks again and again and the pile becomes dominated by small rocks. The sieve is the **environment**, the rocks are individuals with different alleles, and passing through is **surviving and breeding**. It maps the idea that selection removes some variation and shifts the mix. It breaks down because a sieve is fixed and does not create new rocks, whereas real populations also get **new variation from mutation**, and the sieve (the environment) can change.

bullets: **Natural selection**: individuals with characteristics **most suited to the environment** are **more likely to survive and breed successfully**, so the **alleles for those characteristics are passed on** to the next generation.
It is called *natural* because the environment (not humans) does the selecting; compare this with **selective breeding**, where humans choose.

Evolution needs three things: **variation** in the population, characteristics that are **inherited**, and a **selection pressure** that makes some individuals more likely to survive and reproduce than others.
Evolution is **not** goal-directed: organisms do not change because they 'need' to. Variation arises randomly and the environment then filters it.
A change only counts as evolution if it is **inherited** and affects the **population** over **many generations**.
Darwin's simple life forms: the earliest life on Earth was single-celled, and all the diversity today is descended from these ancestors.
Exam link: this point is tested by 'explain how...' questions that want a **chain of reasoning** (variation, survival, breeding, passing on alleles, frequency changes).
core.h: What evolution and natural selection mean
core.p: **Evolution** is a **change in the inherited characteristics of a population over time through a process of natural selection**, which may result in the formation of a **new species**. Charles Darwin's **theory of evolution by natural selection** states that all of the species of living things alive today have **evolved from simple life forms** which first developed over **three billion years ago**. The key word is *population*: individuals do not evolve, they live or die with the genes they were born with, but the make-up of the population changes from generation to generation. Natural selection is the **mechanism** (the how); evolution is the **result** (the what).

bullets: Genetic variation comes from **sexual reproduction** (meiosis shuffles alleles into new combinations, fertilisation combines two parents' genes at random) and from **mutation**.
Environmental variation, such as a scar, a suntan or a plant grown in poor light, is **not inherited** so does not drive evolution.
Most human features, such as height and body mass, are a combination of **genes and environment**: genes set the potential and the environment decides how much is reached.
Different alleles produce different **phenotypes** (the observable characteristics). Selection acts on the **phenotype**, but what is passed on is the **genotype** (alleles).
**Continuous variation** (a range of values such as height) and **discontinuous variation** (distinct categories such as blood group) can both be acted on by selection.
Asexually reproducing organisms produce clones, so they have little variation unless mutation occurs; this is why mutation is so important in bacteria.
A population with **more genetic variation** has a better chance that some individuals survive a change in the environment.
core.h: Variation: the raw material for selection
core.p: **Variation** means the **differences in the characteristics of individuals in a population**. It may be due to differences in the **genes inherited** (genetic causes), the **conditions in which organisms have developed** (environmental causes), or a **combination of both**. For natural selection only the **genetic** part matters, because only inherited differences can be passed on. Without variation there would be nothing for the environment to select between, and every individual would be equally likely to survive.

bullets: Mutations are **random**: they are not caused by the organism 'needing' them, and the environment does not direct which mutation happens.
Most mutations are neutral because of **non-coding DNA** or because the change does not alter the amino acid sequence (a different codon can code for the same amino acid).
A mutation may change the **protein** made, which may change the **shape of an enzyme or other protein** and so the phenotype.
Whether a mutation is 'good' or 'bad' depends on the **environment**: a mutation that is harmful in one environment may be beneficial in another.
Mutation rate can be increased by **ionising radiation** (X-rays, gamma rays, UV) and some chemicals (**mutagens**).
To be passed on, the mutation must occur in a **gamete-forming cell**, or in an asexually reproducing organism such as a bacterium, which passes it to all offspring.
Example: a mutation in a bacterium that makes it **resistant to an antibiotic** is harmless without the antibiotic but gives a huge advantage when the antibiotic is present.
core.h: Mutation: the ultimate source of new alleles
core.p: A **mutation** is a **random change in the base sequence of DNA**. Mutations occur **continuously** in all organisms. Most have **no effect** on the phenotype, some have a **harmful** effect and **very rarely** a mutation leads to a **new phenotype** that gives an advantage. If the new phenotype is **suited to an environmental change**, it can lead to a **relatively rapid change in the species**. Mutation is the only way completely new alleles appear, so it provides the raw variation that sexual reproduction then shuffles.

bullets: Common selection pressures: **predation**, **disease**, **competition** for food, water, light, space and mates, and **changes in climate** such as temperature or rainfall.
**Predation** selects for camouflage, speed, warning colours or defences in prey, and for better senses and speed in predators.
**Competition** within a species (intraspecific) is often fiercest because individuals need exactly the same resources; between species it is interspecific competition.
**Disease** selects for individuals with resistance, such as a rabbit population exposed to myxomatosis.
**Breeding success** matters as much as survival: an organism that lives long but leaves no offspring contributes no alleles to the next generation.
Selection pressures can change over time (for example pollution, new predator, climate change), so what is 'best' also changes.
Link: these are the **biotic and abiotic factors** from the ecology topic (4.7).
core.h: Selection pressures and the struggle for survival
core.p: Organisms usually produce **more offspring than the environment can support**, so there is **competition** for limited resources and many die before they breed. Anything that reduces survival or breeding success is a **selection pressure**. The individuals whose phenotype helps them cope are the ones that survive and breed. This is sometimes described as 'survival of the fittest', where *fittest* means **best suited to the environment and most successful at breeding**, not strongest.

bullets: Step 1: There is **variation** within a population because of differences in **genes** (alleles), caused by sexual reproduction and mutation.
Step 2: **Mutation** may produce a **new allele** and so a new phenotype.
Step 3: There is a **selection pressure** (for example predators, disease, competition, climate), and more offspring are born than can survive.
Step 4: Individuals with the **characteristics best suited to the environment** are **more likely to survive** and **breed successfully**.
Step 5: They **pass on the alleles** for those characteristics to their offspring.
Step 6: Over **many generations** the **frequency of the advantageous allele increases** and the frequency of other alleles decreases.
Step 7: If populations become so different that they **cannot interbreed to produce fertile offspring**, a **new species** has formed.
Models for 6 marks use this exact sequence and link it to a named example.
core.p: Exam answers earn marks for stating each step in order and using the correct terms. The process is a **chain of cause and effect**: variation exists, a selection pressure acts, some individuals survive and breed, the alleles are passed on, and over many generations the proportion of the population with that allele rises. Always say that the **allele** is passed on (or the characteristic is *inherited*), because surviving alone changes nothing unless offspring inherit the advantage.

bullets: Variation: both forms existed in the population, produced originally by mutation.
Selection pressure: **predation by birds** which hunt by sight.
Before pollution: pale moths were **camouflaged**, dark moths were conspicuous and more likely to be eaten, so dark alleles stayed rare.
After pollution: dark moths were camouflaged and survived, bred, and passed on the dark allele, so the **frequency of the dark allele rose**.
After the **Clean Air Acts** in Britain in the 1950s the air cleaned up, lichens returned, and the pale form increased again, showing the direction of selection follows the environment.
Link: the colour difference is due to **alleles**, so it is inherited, unlike a suntan.
Evaluation: experiments in the 1950s supported the idea that birds eat the less well camouflaged form, though later work refined the details.
core.p: The peppered moth exists in a **pale, speckled form** and a **dark (melanic) form**, caused by different alleles. Before the Industrial Revolution most were pale because they were **camouflaged on lichen-covered tree bark**. Soot pollution killed lichens and blackened the trunks in industrial areas, so **dark moths became camouflaged** and **pale moths were easily seen and eaten by birds**. The dark form therefore became far more common in polluted regions. This is a classic example of the environment acting as the selection pressure.

bullets: Mutation produces a resistant strain by chance, before the antibiotic is used.
Antibiotic use is the **selection pressure**: non-resistant bacteria die, resistant bacteria **survive and reproduce**.
Calculation idea: one bacterium dividing every 20 minutes gives 3 divisions per hour, so after 3 hours there are 9 divisions and 2^9 = **512** bacteria, so new strains spread very quickly.
**MRSA** is a bacterium resistant to many antibiotics and is a problem in hospitals.
Resistant strains spread because people are not immune to them and no antibiotic works against them.

To slow the spread: doctors should **not prescribe antibiotics for viral infections or mild bacterial infections**, patients should **complete the full course**, and antibiotics in agriculture should be restricted.
New antibiotics are **expensive and slow to develop**, so the development of resistance is outpacing production of new drugs.
Common error: the bacterium does not 'become used to' the drug; **individuals are either resistant or not**, and selection changes the proportions.
core.p: Bacteria are the clearest modern example because they **reproduce very rapidly** (some can divide about every 20 minutes in ideal conditions). A bacterial population contains variation produced by **mutation**. If a mutation makes a bacterium **resistant** to an antibiotic, then when the antibiotic is used the **non-resistant bacteria are killed** but the resistant ones **survive and reproduce**, passing on the resistance allele. Soon most of the population is resistant. This process is natural selection happening quickly enough to observe, with the antibiotic as the selection pressure.

bullets: **Pesticide-resistant insects**: a few insects have an allele that lets them survive spraying, they breed, and later sprays are less effective.
**Warfarin-resistant rats** appeared in places where warfarin was used as a rat poison, because rats with a resistance allele survived.
**Myxomatosis in rabbits**: the first virus strains killed most rabbits but survivors had inherited resistance and the virus changed over time too.
Evolution applies to the **predator** as well as the prey: if prey get faster, faster predators are favoured.
Why fast reproducers show it quickly: a **short generation time** means many generations pass in a few years.
Humans also face selection pressures, but in large long-lived organisms change takes thousands of generations.
For any example, structure the answer as: variation, selection pressure, survival and breeding, passing on alleles, increased frequency.
core.h: Other examples of rapid natural selection
core.p: Natural selection is visible wherever organisms reproduce quickly and face a strong new selection pressure. Resistance to **pesticides and herbicides** and to **poisons used on pests** shows the same pattern as antibiotic resistance. In each case a rare resistant mutant is already present, the poison removes the non-resistant individuals, and the survivors breed. The result is a population dominated by the resistant allele.

bullets: The **gene pool** is all the alleles in a population.
A beneficial allele starts at a low frequency, then rises generation by generation, producing an S-shaped curve if plotted.
The change in a population is **gradual** but can look sudden if the selection pressure is strong and the generation time is short.
A disadvantageous allele does not usually disappear completely, because it can be hidden in **heterozygous** carriers or reintroduced by mutation.
A population that changes **cannot be undone** by individuals; but if the environment reverses, selection can reverse the trend, as with the pale peppered moth.
Extinction can result if **no individuals** have a phenotype suited to the new environment.
Graph skill: describe trends using numbers, for example 'the percentage of dark moths rose from 2% to 95% over 45 years'.
core.p: A single organism cannot change its genes in response to the environment, so the unit of evolution is the **population**. Natural selection changes **how common each allele is** in the **gene pool**. Individuals either carry an allele or do not; what changes is the **proportion** carrying it. This is why marking schemes ask for 'the **frequency of the allele increases**' or 'more of the population has the characteristic', and why 'the moths changed colour' loses marks.

bullets: Structural: thick fur and blubber in polar animals; camouflage; long roots in desert plants.
Behavioural: migration, hibernation, courtship displays.
Functional: producing antifreeze proteins, antibiotic-resistance enzymes, or the ability of camels to concentrate urine.
A feature is an adaptation because it increases **survival and breeding chances**, so the alleles for it become more common.
A feature that helps in one environment can be a handicap in another (for example a thick coat in a warming climate).
Compromise: adaptations often have costs, such as bright male colouring attracting mates but also predators.
Link: ecology (4.7) asks for named adaptations of organisms in particular habitats; evolution explains how they arose.
core.p: An **adaptation** is a feature that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its habitat. Adaptations may be **structural** (body features), **behavioural** (how the organism acts) or **functional** (how processes work, such as the ability to produce a toxin). Adaptations are **the result of natural selection acting over many generations**, not of an individual deciding to change. 'Fitness' in biology means how well an organism is suited to its environment, measured by how successfully it survives and leaves offspring.

bullets: **Geographical isolation** stops gene flow between the populations.
Different environments give **different selection pressures**, so different alleles are favoured.
Different mutations arise in each population independently.
After enough time the populations cannot produce **fertile** offspring (for example a horse and donkey produce a sterile mule, so they are different species).
Speciation takes **very many generations**, often thousands or millions of years.
Alfred Russel Wallace independently proposed the same idea and gathered evidence for natural selection and speciation; the full treatment is in the 'Theories of evolution and speciation' note.
Higher-style answer: describe isolation, different selection pressures, different alleles, and inability to produce fertile offspring.
core.p: A **species** is a group of organisms that can **interbreed to produce fertile offspring**. If two populations of one species become so different in **phenotype** that they can **no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring**, they are **two different species**. This is usually helped by **isolation**: a physical barrier such as a mountain range, sea or river separates the populations, so they cannot exchange genes. Each population then experiences different selection pressures and mutations, and over many generations they diverge.

bullets: Fossils: remains of organisms from millions of years ago found in rocks; they show changes in features over time and extinct species.
The fossil record is **incomplete** because early life forms were soft-bodied (few traces), fossils are destroyed by geological activity, and many were never found.
Observed evolution: antibiotic-resistant bacteria, pesticide-resistant insects and the peppered moth.
Genetic evidence: similarities in DNA and proteins between species reflect common ancestry and allow classification.
Darwin's theory was widely accepted only after the discovery of **genes** gave a mechanism for inheritance and variation.
Evidence must be **valid** and **repeatable**; science changes theories as new evidence emerges.
Link: Darwin's voyage and his observations of variation between related species were his starting evidence.
core.p: The theory is supported by several independent lines of evidence. **Fossils** show how organisms have changed over very long periods, and they appear in rocks in an order that matches their age. **Resistant bacteria** show natural selection happening within a human lifetime. **DNA comparisons** show that species thought to be closely related have more similar DNA, supporting the idea of shared ancestors. When different kinds of evidence agree, scientists have more confidence in the theory.

bullets: Individuals do **not** change in response to need: variation is already present and the environment selects.
Acquired characteristics (a bodybuilder's muscles) are **not inherited**; this was Lamarck's idea, which has been rejected.
'Survival of the fittest' does not mean the strongest, but those best **suited to the environment** and best at **breeding**.
Mutation does not happen *because* of selection pressure; selection acts after the mutation exists.

Links: **genetics** (alleles, meiosis, inheritance), **ecology** (competition, adaptations), **infection and response** (antibiotic resistance), **selective breeding** (artificial selection) and **classification**.
Selective breeding differs from natural selection because **humans** decide which individuals breed, for traits useful to people.
Ethical angle: human use of antibiotics speeds up the evolution of resistance, so personal choices have population-level effects.
core.h: Common misconceptions and links to other topics
core.p: Many errors on this topic come from using everyday language rather than biological language. Examiners want you to avoid purposeful words such as 'needed', 'wanted', 'tried to' or 'adapted themselves'. Strong answers always talk about **alleles**, **variation**, **survival**, **breeding** and **generations**. Evolution also connects to genetics, ecology, health and classification, so it can appear in synoptic questions.

exam: 'Explain how natural selection...' (usually 4 to 6 marks): write a chain: **variation** (alleles) → **selection pressure** → those best suited **survive and breed** → **pass on alleles** → **frequency increases** over generations. Each link can earn a mark.
Use the phrase **'more likely to survive and breed successfully'**, not 'survive' alone.
Say **'allele'** or **'gene'** is passed on; examiners reject 'the characteristic was passed on' only when vague, but 'allele' is safest.
For **2 mark** questions, give one cause and one consequence, for example: 'Dark moths were camouflaged so less likely to be eaten, so more bred and passed on the allele.'
Define evolution in 2 marks: 'change in inherited characteristics of a population' (1) 'over time/many generations through natural selection' (1).
For **antibiotic resistance** questions, include mutation, antibiotic as selection pressure, resistant survive, reproduce, pass on resistance, population becomes resistant (6 marks).
For **data questions**, quote values from the table or graph with units and calculate the change (percentage or percentage points) using ((new − old) ÷ old) × 100.
Command words: **Describe** = what happens; **Explain** = why it happens, using science; **Suggest** = apply your knowledge to an unfamiliar example.
Do not use purposeful language ('wanted to', 'in order to survive'); use passive scientific phrasing ('were better adapted to').
For **speciation**, include isolation, different selection pressures, and inability to produce **fertile** offspring.
Check units and the wording 'percentage points' versus 'percent' when comparing percentages.

mistakes.r: Moths cannot change colour. Moths already existed in two forms; the camouflaged form survived and bred, so its allele became more common.
mistakes.w: The moths changed colour to match the trees.

mistakes.r: A random mutation gives resistance to some bacteria; the antibiotic kills the non-resistant ones; the resistant survivors reproduce and pass on the allele.
mistakes.w: Bacteria become resistant because they get used to the antibiotic.

mistakes.r: There was variation in neck length (due to alleles); the longer-necked individuals were more likely to survive and breed and passed on the alleles.
mistakes.w: The animals needed longer necks so they grew them.

mistakes.r: Populations evolve. Individuals keep the genes they were born with; the frequency of alleles in the population changes.
Fittest means best suited to the environment, including breeding successfully and passing on alleles.
mistakes.w: Survival of the fittest means the strongest survives.

mistakes.r: Mutations are random. They happen continuously; the environment only decides whether the new phenotype helps survival.
mistakes.w: Mutations happen because the organism needs them.

mistakes.r: State that they survived, bred and passed on the allele, so the proportion of dark moths in the next generation increased.
mistakes.w: The moths with the dark colour survived (and nothing more).

mistakes.r: Acquired characteristics are not inherited; only changes in genes are passed on.
mistakes.w: Characteristics gained in life, like big muscles, are passed on.

mistakes.r: A scientific theory is supported by a large amount of evidence (fossils, DNA, observed resistance) and explains observations.
mistakes.w: Evolution is only a theory, so it is just a guess.

summary: You must know that Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection explains how all living things evolved from simple life forms over more than three billion years: variation exists (from mutation and sexual reproduction), individuals best suited to the environment survive and breed, and they pass on their alleles. You must be able to apply this to peppered moths and antibiotic-resistant bacteria and explain how new species form. It matters because it underpins genetics, ecology, medicine (resistance) and much of the exam's 6-mark reasoning.

terms.d: A change in the inherited characteristics of a population over time through a process of natural selection which may result in the formation of a new species.
The process by which individuals with characteristics most suited to the environment are more likely to survive and breed successfully, passing on the alleles for those characteristics.
Differences in the characteristics of individuals in a population, caused by genes, the environment, or both.
A random change in the base sequence of DNA that may produce a new allele and sometimes a new phenotype.
A different version of the same gene.
All the alleles present in a population.
An environmental factor, such as predation, disease or competition, that affects the chance of survival and breeding.
A group of organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
The formation of a new species when populations become so different they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
A feature of an organism that increases its chance of survival and reproduction in its environment.
The observable characteristics of an organism, produced by its genes and the environment.
The combination of alleles an organism has for a gene.
The ability of bacteria to survive an antibiotic because of a mutation, which is passed on to offspring.
Separation of populations (for example by a physical barrier) so that they cannot interbreed.
Organisms of the same or different species trying to obtain the same limited resources.
When no individuals of a species remain alive.
The preserved remains or traces of organisms from many thousands or millions of years ago, found in rocks.

worked.ans: Model answer: Moths show variation caused by different alleles. When soot darkened the bark, dark moths were better camouflaged and less likely to be eaten by birds, so they were more likely to survive and breed. They passed on the allele for dark colour to their offspring, so over many generations the proportion of dark moths in the population increased.
worked.q: Before 1850 almost all peppered moths near a city were pale. By 1895 most were dark. Explain this change in the population using natural selection. (6 marks)
steps: Variation: both pale and dark moths existed because of different alleles (the dark allele arose by mutation).
Selection pressure: soot darkened tree bark; birds hunt moths by sight.
Dark moths were camouflaged so were less likely to be eaten; pale moths were easily seen and eaten.
Dark moths were more likely to survive and breed successfully.
They passed on the dark allele to their offspring.
Over many generations the frequency of the dark allele increased, so most of the population became dark.

worked.ans: A mutation gives some bacteria resistance. When the antibiotic is used, non-resistant bacteria die but resistant bacteria survive and reproduce, passing on the resistance allele, so the population becomes mainly resistant.
worked.q: Explain how a population of bacteria becomes resistant to an antibiotic. (4 marks)
steps: A random mutation produces a resistant bacterium.
The antibiotic kills the non-resistant bacteria.
The resistant bacteria survive and reproduce, passing the allele on.
The proportion of resistant bacteria increases; population becomes resistant.
